<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-cache-engineering-55c07860" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0c6d6f970c0c9373">Why can a long-running agent keep its chat history while running out of inference cache memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acache-engineering">Cache Engineering for Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Logical conversation stores text, while KV cache stores each layer&#x27;s intermediate representations of past tokens. Their purpose and footprint differ. Longer conversation increases cache memory and subsequent reads. Cache Engineering manages that state directly while preserving logical history, but recovering evicted cache still costs computation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Ten thousand tool-log lines can remain in the conversation even while their KV is inactive. Reusing those logs later can require recomputing representations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28577">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.28577-cache-engineering/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0c6d6f970c0c9373">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:cache-engineering" data-paper-title="Cache Engineering for Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-32449a79dfd682e3">Why can the same final text prefix correspond to different, nonreusable KV caches?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acache-engineering">Cache Engineering for Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>KV depends on the history and positions visible when it was computed. Dropping tokens at different times can alter later states. repos must also transform RoPE keys for their new positions; updating indices alone or rotating values is wrong. Cache identity must therefore track position versions and operation history, not just logical text.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Evicting a tool response before generation versus afterward changes what later tokens could see. Matching final retained text does not make those caches interchangeable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28577">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.28577-cache-engineering/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-32449a79dfd682e3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:cache-engineering" data-paper-title="Cache Engineering for Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a73d4740f29bdb97">How does direct KV management differ from summarizing text for recovery and reuse?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acache-engineering">Cache Engineering for Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Summarization changes logical input and can invalidate later KV, requiring fresh prefill. Direct management preserves logical history but changes active state and position versions. Different operation timing can produce different KV for the same final text and token set, so cache reuse identity must include history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Dropping tool KV before versus after generating a sentence can change that sentence&#x27;s hidden state even when the final retained text is identical.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28577">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.28577-cache-engineering/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a73d4740f29bdb97">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:cache-engineering" data-paper-title="Cache Engineering for Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-20470428e0e80972">Why does repos rotate keys but not apply the same RoPE transform to values?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acache-engineering">Cache Engineering for Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tsinghua University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Moving a position from p to q adjusts an already rotated key by R(q)R(p)^-1, while the value stays unchanged. drop itself does not renumber. The cache system also needs operation history and versions. The local run does not implement AKV or serving; a few tensor rotations are not full cache engineering.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Moving a key from position ten to five undoes the old rotation and applies the new one. Rotating its value would change how its content is read.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 成本与复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28577">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.28577-cache-engineering/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-20470428e0e80972">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:tokenworth" data-paper-title="Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-tokenworth-16bf712f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f2c0104195a8c16b">Should the most related memories always be kept, and what resource limits does TokenWorth face?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atokenworth">Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Memory capacity, interactions, and generation length are finite. A long, superficially relevant memory can crowd out more useful information. TokenWorth treats retention and use as value allocation under resource competition rather than maximizing library size or similarity alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A long guide repeats known steps, while a short note records a key permission restriction. The shorter note can deserve a slot despite weaker word overlap.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26453">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.26453-tokenworth/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f2c0104195a8c16b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:tokenworth" data-paper-title="Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-339227d3e489e486">Why use one memory-worth model for both retrieval and eviction rather than rank only by similarity?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atokenworth">Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Similar memories may be long, obsolete, or unreliable. Under budget, compare actual task value. Stable base features supply interpretable signals, and RFM learns a query-dependent residual. The same value scale guides retrieval and retention. Feedback updates only memories actually selected and used; do not invent outcomes for unvisited entries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two memories concern the same interface. The old one is more similar but obsolete; the newer one is shorter and reliable, and may be worth retaining instead.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26453">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.26453-tokenworth/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-339227d3e489e486">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:tokenworth" data-paper-title="Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a8e4f6ea933a6baa">Why separate fast residual fitting from slow feature-geometry updates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atokenworth">Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fast updates fit value discrepancies from new feedback promptly. Slow updates use gradient statistics to adapt kernel-distance geometry without large representation swings after every observation. These are different adaptation timescales. The residual model cannot see all candidate outcomes; only used memory pairs have real labels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: One failure can lower a memory&#x27;s residual worth. Multiple feedback observations can later change which feature differences the kernel amplifies.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26453">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.26453-tokenworth/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a8e4f6ea933a6baa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:tokenworth" data-paper-title="Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0647c429cb8f101e">Why can a newly admitted memory still be evicted immediately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atokenworth">Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanjing University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Admission checks novelty or probe value relative to the best old memory. The expanded library then evicts the lowest overall value, and the new item competes too. Probes use real current and historical queries, not future test questions. Only selected pairs receive updates, not invented counterfactual success labels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A sufficiently novel candidate enters a full library but ranks last by shared value. It should leave rather than force out a stronger existing memory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26453">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.26453-tokenworth/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0647c429cb8f101e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memprice" data-paper-title="MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memprice-d97f4c90" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-64958fe98e9312aa">Why are MemPrice&#x27;s five representation levels a joint allocation problem?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemprice">MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hong Kong University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each memory can be full text, summary, abstraction, keywords, or deletion. These differ in size and usefulness and compete for one hard token budget. Independently picking the best version can exceed capacity. Optimize jointly while choosing at most one per item; deleted detail cannot be reconstructed from nothing in the current window.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: One full-text memory can crowd out two summaries. Compare the whole group instead of choosing highest fidelity independently for every item.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24955">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.24955-memprice/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-64958fe98e9312aa">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memprice" data-paper-title="MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-29f54f6e9186beb3">Why shouldn&#x27;t an archive refresh reset the virtual queue and global round count?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemprice">MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hong Kong University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The queue represents cumulative resource pressure, and the round count scales the dynamic price. Refresh only extracts a new representation from an external archive. Resetting both would forget past overuse and suddenly underprice detail. Hard capacity still applies every round; an average occupancy target cannot replace it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: After several nearly full context windows, a summary refresh should not zero the price and cause another wave of expensive full-text retention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24955">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.24955-memprice/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-29f54f6e9186beb3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memprice" data-paper-title="MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-cfac8a0fe4b552e0">How does dynamic pricing represent long-run capacity pressure that relevance Top-K misses?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemprice">MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hong Kong University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Top-K uses only the current ranking. Dynamic price comes from a virtual queue of persistent occupancy, so historical overuse makes retaining detail more expensive. Hard capacity caps one round; average occupancy controls long-run pressure. They are not the same threshold, and the mechanism does not guarantee global optimality for all state paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Repeatedly filling the window raises the price and encourages lower fidelity. A currently relevant memory may no longer justify keeping a long original.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24955">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.24955-memprice/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cfac8a0fe4b552e0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memprice" data-paper-title="MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c7546f168cfded3">How does MemPrice fit each memory&#x27;s alternatives into a hard token budget?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemprice">MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hong Kong University of Science and Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Enumerate full text, summary, abstraction, keywords, and deletion, then measure sizes with the tokenizer. Use multiple-choice knapsack to choose at most one representation per memory. Each round must stay within B. The average occupancy target changes price, not whether the current window may exceed capacity. Archive refresh does not invent deleted detail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: With one hundred tokens left and two eighty-token originals, select summaries if useful instead of combining the independently best originals.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24955">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.24955-memprice/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c7546f168cfded3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:proper-agent" data-paper-title="MemoProAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-proper-agent-67e59e1f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c6fb8b73132c6f21">Why must MemoProAgent make one more judgment than ordinary QA when no user asks a question?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aproper-agent">MemoProAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Michigan State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>QA starts with a request. A proactive assistant must also decide whether to interrupt now, what to mention, and whether it has already said it. The paper combines long-term experience with current visual context to help at the right moment rather than maximize message count. Correct reminders can still fail through bad timing or repetition.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Reminding someone to bring keys before leaving can help. Repeating it three times after they already picked them up does not.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22671v2">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.22671-proper-agent/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c6fb8b73132c6f21">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:proper-agent" data-paper-title="MemoProAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-045d69d686b724af">Why does a proactive assistant need a separate intervention gate after retrieving relevant memories?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aproper-agent">MemoProAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Michigan State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Relevance means topical overlap, not that interrupting now is warranted. The gate decides whether evidence merits intervention; the generator uses the current scene and prior speech to speak or stay silent. Timing and count matter, so correct but late or repeated reminders are not perfect success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A nut allergy is relevant when the food is visible and the assistant has not warned yet. Repeating the warning creates a false trigger.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22671v2">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.22671-proper-agent/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-045d69d686b724af">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:proper-agent" data-paper-title="MemoProAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e48b4ca5f13b843f">Why do Perfect and a Hit for saying the right thing at least once measure different behavior?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aproper-agent">MemoProAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Michigan State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Perfect requires correct content within the trigger window and exactly one utterance. Hit does not rule out early, late, or repeated interruption. Any speech on a silent negative segment is a false trigger. Raising recall alone can hurt user experience; content hits do not replace timing and count evaluation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An early reminder followed by another inside the window can count as a hit without being a perfect intervention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22671v2">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.22671-proper-agent/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e48b4ca5f13b843f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:proper-agent" data-paper-title="MemoProAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d55e6f3085127031">Can PPR retrieval and the semantic gate be replaced by one open-loop flag?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aproper-agent">MemoProAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Michigan State University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. PPR performs actual personalized random walks with restart on entity relations. The gate decides whether the retrieved evidence warrants intervention. Training optimizes only generator tokens, not tool-injected evidence. A local fixture is not the official evaluation on authorized long videos and cannot use a flag to supply the right utterance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Retrieving a relation between a cup and drinking habits still leaves the gate to determine whether the user just drank. The relation alone is not permission to speak.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22671v2">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.22671-proper-agent/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d55e6f3085127031">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memscope" data-paper-title="MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memscope-50996985" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7cf2a5900fc62d97">Why does MemScope inspect raw trajectories, runtime memory, and provider code together?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemscope">MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences / University of Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The same failure can come from writing, retrieval, or use, which a total score cannot distinguish. Traces show actions, memory shows stored contents, and code explains the rules. Together they support a bounded repair. If evidence is insufficient, return no-patch rather than forcing edits every round.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A fact written but never retrieved requires a different fix than a fact never written. A wrong answer alone does not distinguish them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21170">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.21170-memscope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7cf2a5900fc62d97">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memscope" data-paper-title="MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-5218d2bd32d78c40">Why doesn&#x27;t an unchanged memory-provider signature prove a patch is compatible with existing memories?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemscope">MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences / University of Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A signature constrains call shape, not internal field meanings or read/write semantics. MemScope combines raw traces, runtime memory, and code, patches in a bounded transaction, and probes real formats. Failure must preserve old code and memory; insufficient evidence can also mean no patch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: The parameter is still named memory, but a patch changes timestamps from seconds to days. Old records can be misread even though the code passes syntax checks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21170">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.21170-memscope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5218d2bd32d78c40">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memscope" data-paper-title="MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-eb6033fa16a8e137">What is the trade-off between an in-place patch and regenerating the whole memory provider?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemscope">MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences / University of Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A local edit preserves provider identity and reduces compatibility and format drift. Keeping the interface still does not guarantee unchanged semantics, so run real probes. A full rewrite gives more freedom but can make old memory uninterpretable. Lines of code do not measure either strategy&#x27;s effectiveness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Adjusting a retrieval threshold can preserve stored records. Replacing the schema without migration may silently ignore them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21170">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.21170-memscope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eb6033fa16a8e137">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memscope" data-paper-title="MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c63246984a392d8f">Why must replaceOnce match exactly once, and why allow no-patch when evidence is weak?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemscope">MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences / University of Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A local patch must identify the intended logic. Replacing arbitrary duplicate text can change the wrong behavior. replaceOnce requires a unique target and respects interface identity, syntax, and edit budgets. If localization or probe evidence is weak, do not submit a patch. Engineering validity alone is not semantic improvement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two sites have identical field reads. A patch specifying only that string cannot disambiguate them, so decline instead of changing the first match.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 成本与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21170">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.21170-memscope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c63246984a392d8f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hy-memory" data-paper-title="Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-hy-memory-1a0f6bb8" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4283a29efc1ef0b5">Why are storing every conversation and writing memories for future questions different tasks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahy-memory">Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent Hunyuan</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raw conversations are large and later readers have limited context. A writer must preserve usable facts and relationships while controlling storage growth. Hy-Memory trains that policy rather than merely enlarging the archive. The useful test is whether later answers can be grounded in the resulting memory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A discussion reschedules a meeting repeatedly. A later question needs the final date and its confirmation, not a mechanical archive of every repeated message.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22196">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.22196-hy-memory/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4283a29efc1ef0b5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hy-memory" data-paper-title="Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4e2c519e59efd8df">Why freeze the reader and judge before optimizing the memory writer?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahy-memory">Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent Hunyuan</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Changing reader and judge together confounds better writing with stronger reading. Holding them fixed lets chunk probes and factual attribution isolate writer contributions; a storage-growth penalty prevents keeping everything. Each rollout gets one vote per chunk. More calls are not more independent evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Give both writers&#x27; outputs to the same reader. Differences better reflect which facts were retained than whether one writer happened to get a stronger answer model.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22196">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.22196-hy-memory/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4e2c519e59efd8df">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hy-memory" data-paper-title="Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-6f446465268432d1">Why use both per-chunk probes and final outcome rewards?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahy-memory">Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent Hunyuan</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Final answer feedback is sparse. Chunk probes give nearer signals about writing quality, and cross-chunk attribution estimates factual contributions. A growth penalty discourages storing everything. High local probe scores do not ensure cross-session answers, and a final outcome alone cannot identify the useful write.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An early chunk saves the right date, then a later chunk overwrites it incorrectly. Local probes and final attribution need to reveal the damage together.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22196">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.22196-hy-memory/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6f446465268432d1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hy-memory" data-paper-title="Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-791e7424953c1d9b">Can multiple calls for the same chunk count as multiple reward votes?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahy-memory">Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent Hunyuan</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Each rollout casts one vote per chunk, and advantages are normalized within chunk groups. Counting calls would give extra influence to more active trajectories. Gold stays with the judge, not writer, reader, or retrieval query. Large-scale writer RL was not run locally.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Five calls checking one chunk and one call in another rollout still contribute one vote each, not five versus one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22196">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.22196-hy-memory/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-791e7424953c1d9b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:transparent-compact" data-paper-title="Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-transparent-compact-55d09739" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-eba8a2358514944d">Why are user commitments and constraints especially easy to lose when compressing long coding sessions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atransparent-compact">Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hokkaido University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Large tool logs and discussions compete for context. Summaries can omit small but binding phrases or turn conditional requests into unconditional ones. Transparent compression marks what stays and what moves, with a path back to original materials, so continuation knows what is visible and what needs retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: &#x27;Submit only after confirming tests&#x27; summarized as &#x27;prepare to submit&#x27; can make a later agent mistake conditional permission for unconditional authorization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20116">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.20116-transparent-compact/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eba8a2358514944d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:transparent-compact" data-paper-title="Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4625d241bccf4365">Why are verbatim messages and omission markers more transparent than a fluent regenerated summary?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atransparent-compact">Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hokkaido University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Verbatim text preserves commitment wording. Omission markers identify what was moved out and provide a route back to the full conversation. This avoids silently turning guesses into facts. A recovery index does not mean the model found the evidence, and historical search can require paid subagent inference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Summarizing &#x27;do not deploy for now&#x27; without &#x27;for now&#x27; changes the requirement. Keeping the original wording and marking removed tool logs makes the compression easier to audit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20116">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.20116-transparent-compact/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4625d241bccf4365">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:transparent-compact" data-paper-title="Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8116fd9b483b9d71">Why can&#x27;t deterministic compression and model-subagent context_lookup both be called zero-call?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atransparent-compact">Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hokkaido University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compression rules need no model, but semantic historical search uses a model subagent and has separate capability and cost. The local run restores exact IDs and checks hashes, not the paper&#x27;s model retrieval. Fewer visible characters indicate a view change, not memory-QA ability or proportional total storage savings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Reading a log by its known ID is model-free. Finding which commitment matters without an ID may need extra inference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20116">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.20116-transparent-compact/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8116fd9b483b9d71">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:transparent-compact" data-paper-title="Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f938ecc9e7878519">Why must Pi branch structure and tool metadata survive even when body text is removed?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Atransparent-compact">Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Hokkaido University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Read only ancestors of the chosen leaf so sibling histories cannot leak in. Tool pairing IDs, names, errors, and exit states preserve invocation semantics after body removal. A character cap evicts the oldest full blocks and leaves recovery markers, so the active context no longer contains every original statement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Preserve isError=false rather than treating false as missing; otherwise later compression can lose proof the call succeeded.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 代码映射与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20116">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.20116-transparent-compact/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f938ecc9e7878519">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:formcraft" data-paper-title="Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-formcraft-179a4f71" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f08554ccb6cff842">What distinguishes a first-class composite capability from a stored formation history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aformcraft">Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · not listed in paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A first-class capability has its own type, public call ID, and execution semantics, so it is a candidate in later compositions. Formation history records how it was assembled and may require searching again. Direct reuse avoids formation work, but still runs recursive computation on the current input rather than caching an old answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Append 01 can become an ordinary operator by ID. It still appends both items to today&#x27;s input, not returning yesterday&#x27;s result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19414">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.19414-formcraft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f08554ccb6cff842">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:formcraft" data-paper-title="Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3b8c5d9187005269">Why separate forming a composite capability from admitting it to a persistent skill library?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aformcraft">Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · not listed in paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compatible interfaces show that operations compose, not that the composition meets intended behavior. Independent validation gates admission. Persistent identity binds parents, types, and composition, while loading checks references and acyclicity. Later direct invocation saves search, not the real underlying computation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Sorting then deduplicating can be wired together but may fail on empty input. Validate before storing it for direct reuse.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19414">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.19414-formcraft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3b8c5d9187005269">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:formcraft" data-paper-title="Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c17b37b142fb2068">What work does invoking an admitted composite save over expanding and searching again?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aformcraft">Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · not listed in paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A first-class composite can participate as a typed operation with an identity, so later tasks do not repeat formation search. Expanding again must recover parent operations and wiring. Reuse saves search and assembly, while inner computation still runs. Count calls, formation attempts, and underlying work separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Reuse a learned filter-then-sort operation directly. Filtering and sorting still execute; skipping assembly does not make them free.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19414">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.19414-formcraft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c17b37b142fb2068">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:formcraft" data-paper-title="Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-22e0a1a33b08c7e5">Why recheck the canonical hash, parent references, and acyclicity on cold load?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aformcraft">Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · not listed in paper</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Persistent identity comes from canonical JSON of types, operations, and parent IDs. Files can be corrupted or tampered with. Complete parent references and acyclicity ensure legal recursion. True persistence testing destroys the old object and cold-loads the same snapshot. A local sequence-domain result is not general Lean or LLM capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A file can set its own ID as a parent without changing its name, creating a cycle. Keeping a live object in memory does not verify recovery from disk.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 代码映射、验证与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19414">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.19414-formcraft/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-22e0a1a33b08c7e5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:t2mem" data-paper-title="Test-Time Memory Construction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-t2mem-26ea91d6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-94d7075589ae1f65">Why store only lightweight metadata offline and build detailed memory at query time?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3At2mem">Test-Time Memory Construction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>What matters in a conversation depends on the question, and an offline summary can discard details too early. Event metadata retains lookup clues and raw links. SearchMeta, ReadRaw, and Answer build a query-specific cache at inference. Multiple accesses still cost work; this is not zero memory processing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: To answer an old travel-date question, find the event index and then read the source conversation rather than prewriting one universal summary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13348">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13348-t2mem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-94d7075589ae1f65">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:t2mem" data-paper-title="Test-Time Memory Construction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b0c127555f8d8377">Why does ReadRaw only accept metadata IDs that have already been observed?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3At2mem">Test-Time Memory Construction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Lightweight metadata provides traceable entry points. Reading raw text must bind to IDs actually returned, preventing fabricated links or access to unauthorized records. Memory builds for the current question through alternating search, reading, and answering. The metadata index is not fully understood memory and must not carry the final answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Search returns meeting M7, so ReadRaw can open its conversation. A model-invented M999 is not valid historical evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13348">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13348-t2mem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b0c127555f8d8377">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:t2mem" data-paper-title="Test-Time Memory Construction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-27318e8b4bfc56e5">How does test-time memory construction differ from one retrieval with fixed context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3At2mem">Test-Time Memory Construction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One retrieval fixes evidence before later gaps are known. Test-time construction updates memory alongside information needs and can search or read more. This grants tool autonomy but can also waste steps; evaluate whether it improves real answers, not just action execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A meeting mentions rescheduling. Search for a subsequent event to confirm the new date instead of clinging to the date retrieved first.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13348">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13348-t2mem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-27318e8b4bfc56e5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:t2mem" data-paper-title="Test-Time Memory Construction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e80d57b9c393e851">What state is managed by excluding seen entries in SearchMeta versus appending to the query cache?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3At2mem">Test-Time Memory Construction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northeastern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Seen entries record metadata IDs already returned and prevent duplicate results in this question. The cache accumulates useful material obtained for reasoning and answering. Raw conversations remain traceable external sources; the cache is not a prefilled answer. Separate states let you check whether search gains information and trace answer evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Once meeting A&#x27;s entry is seen, search should seek other events. Keep A&#x27;s decision in the cache after reading it; skipping its entry does not erase evidence already read.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 结果、验证与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13348">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13348-t2mem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e80d57b9c393e851">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:near" data-paper-title="NEAR: Neighborhood-Aware Residuals for Memory Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-near-5f289457" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6332ddad35451607">Why is the actual clue harder to find when many memories discuss the same person or project?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Anear">NEAR: Neighborhood-Aware Residuals for Memory Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Whole-record representations can be dominated by common topics. Frequent names make records similar and bury rare dates or events. NEAR uses neighborhood relations to emphasize distinctions and retrieve specific facts rather than repeatedly retrieving topical material.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Ten records mention project A, but only one says it moved to Thursday. A date question needs that difference, not more mentions of the name.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13314">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13314-near/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6332ddad35451607">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:near" data-paper-title="NEAR: Neighborhood-Aware Residuals for Memory Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8d0178f13d458596">Why might subtracting the neighbor mean direction help find memories with unique facts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Anear">NEAR: Neighborhood-Aware Residuals for Memory Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Neighbors often share names and topics, making irrelevant entries similar. Projecting out the shared direction highlights distinguishing residuals. Queries use a precomputed reference table, not relevance labels to choose a direction. Residuals can remove useful shared clues too, so retain the original view and choose fusion on development data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two records mention the same business trip, but only one says the return is Friday. Suppressing the common trip direction can make the return fact matter more.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13314">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13314-near/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8d0178f13d458596">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:near" data-paper-title="NEAR: Neighborhood-Aware Residuals for Memory Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-25b6ffcabe1f2f25">How do removing a shared direction and training a query-only adapter differ in their information sources?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Anear">NEAR: Neighborhood-Aware Residuals for Memory Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>NEAR constructs memory references, scales, and its small table only from memory states, with no query labels. A query gets its direction from the anchor table. Supervised adapters use training relevance to update query transforms. These are different information contracts; an unlabeled reference did not learn an answer-specific direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Memory neighborhoods can be built without query answers. Choosing a reference because it is the correct evidence would introduce supervision leakage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13314">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13314-near/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-25b6ffcabe1f2f25">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:near" data-paper-title="NEAR: Neighborhood-Aware Residuals for Memory Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3bcdaa3f17a002c4">Why not L2-normalize the whole concatenated vector after fusing layers?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Anear">NEAR: Neighborhood-Aware Residuals for Memory Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Layer scores are scaled by memory–memory population variance and weighted. Concatenation coefficients make one dot product equal the fusion formula. Global normalization adds a sample-dependent denominator and changes ranking. Variance includes self-similarity, and neighborhoods are recomputed on normalized residuals at each layer rather than reused from layer one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two memories have different concatenated norms. Unit normalization penalizes the larger norm, so scores no longer equal the chosen linear combination.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 代码映射与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13314">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13314-near/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3bcdaa3f17a002c4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:beyond-final-embedding" data-paper-title="Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-beyond-final-embedding-06288f14" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
