<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-9b251eeae4e985d6">Why can a pooled embedding miss a local fact in memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abeyond-final-embedding">Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pooling compresses several facts into one vector, so a date or object difference can be drowned out by a shared topic. Final-layer content tokens retain finer contextual evidence for sparse matching. A token match is not an independent dictionary meaning or guaranteed fact; combine it with the global branch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two records discuss travel, but only one sentence states a rebooking date. Their pooled vectors can be close while the local date token distinguishes them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13277">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13277-beyond-final-embedding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9b251eeae4e985d6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:beyond-final-embedding" data-paper-title="Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-84ba9ade85040011">Why is global token top-k followed by memory-ID aggregation different from per-memory MaxSim?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abeyond-final-embedding">Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>In global retrieval, tokens from all memories compete for a sparse return budget. MaxSim per record searches matches independently, changing computation and candidate distributions. Unreturned positions use a shared floor rather than true zero evidence. The pooled branch preserves overall meaning and can surface a memory without retrieved local tokens.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: One record contains a rare date that strongly matches the question. Global token search can retrieve the date then its record without first ranking the pooled record highest.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13277">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13277-beyond-final-embedding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-84ba9ade85040011">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:beyond-final-embedding" data-paper-title="Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0cd43e87a4cab556">Which representations change with a query-only adapter versus retraining the memory encoder?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abeyond-final-embedding">Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Query-only training freezes the encoder and memory bank and applies a low-rank residual to query content tokens, adapting them to existing geometry. Retraining the encoder can move both sides and require re-encoding old memory under a consistent version. The smaller update cannot restore information already lost in encoding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keep a million memory vectors fixed and adjust the query for who approved on Tuesday. Updating the shared encoder may require recomputing all old vectors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13277">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13277-beyond-final-embedding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0cd43e87a4cab556">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:beyond-final-embedding" data-paper-title="Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e579e1a374e3da19">Why doesn&#x27;t the query adapter backpropagate through discrete neighbor selection?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abeyond-final-embedding">Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Southeast University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Training uses multi-positive cross-entropy on all-memory MaxSim as a continuous surrogate; inference uses sparse token search. Discrete ANN selection does not supply a valid gradient. The low-rank residual adjusts only query content tokens while preserving norm. Encoder, memory bank, and pooled query stay frozen; validation alone chooses hyperparameters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Top-K indices jump when a query changes, so they cannot be differentiated as a smooth function. Train on differentiable full matching, then use the sparse index at inference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 数据协议、结果与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13277">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.13277-beyond-final-embedding/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e579e1a374e3da19">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hippocam" data-paper-title="Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-hippocam-33da2b45" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0dd2936011497890">How do nested intentions differ from an ordinary rolling summary?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahippocam">Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Nested intentions organize current goals and subgoals. Experiences are abstracted when their intent closes, whereas rolling summaries compress primarily by time and need not know whether a task finished. Hippocam keeps an original-message tree and recalls one layer at a time, retaining traceability after abstraction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Dependency checks can finish within an unresolved debugging goal. Summarize the closed subgoal without archiving the whole task as complete.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.12124-hippocam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0dd2936011497890">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hippocam" data-paper-title="Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f958509ffcb6e00a">Why does hierarchical recall return one layer at a time rather than immediately expanding all raw history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahippocam">Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Upper-level narratives give purpose and structure first, letting the agent drill down only when needed instead of refilling context each time. Original messages remain in child nodes, so abstraction is reversible. Reserve budget for the next turn and explicitly fail if protected complete exchanges still do not fit, rather than silently truncating them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An upper node says login was repaired last week. Expand the log children only when checking the error, without returning every debug output.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.12124-hippocam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f958509ffcb6e00a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hippocam" data-paper-title="Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8a074b4ab31f5006">Why does it matter that Precip triggers after the response but before the tool result?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahippocam">Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The placement lets the system process closed intentions from the completed main response without assuming an observation that has not arrived. Tool exchanges must remain complete; compression cannot split an unfinished call. Trigger timing is a state contract, not interchangeable with inserting a summary anywhere.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: After a tool call is issued but before its result arrives, do not summarize it as a successful verification. Wait until the real observation enters a later exchange.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.12124-hippocam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8a074b4ab31f5006">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hippocam" data-paper-title="Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d3449f814ee2415f">Do three archives in a controlled pressure probe show autonomous learning of intent closure?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahippocam">Use and Disuse: Intent-Structured Experience Consolidation for Memory and Learning in LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Three real autonomous tasks produced no closure and zero archives. The separate controlled probe verifies pressure handling and protection only. Include request overhead and the next-turn estimate in budget. If protecting K complete exchanges and the dynamic window exceeds capacity, fail before main inference rather than truncate silently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A predefined closure signal exercises Palim. It does not show that a model emits the signal on unknown tasks; report these runs separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 验证与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12124">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.12124-hippocam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d3449f814ee2415f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:mem-plus-plus" data-paper-title="Mem++: Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term Organizational LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-mem-plus-plus-c101fe19" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-107269a5af712c2f">Why do Mem++ non-destructive writes retain date and author?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amem-plus-plus">Mem++: Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term Organizational LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The University of Texas at Austin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Original text carries facts, date supports as-of queries and version selection, and author preserves provenance and context. The write does not irreversibly rewrite records with a model, so later questions can reinterpret them. Raw storage does not guarantee retrieval and costs more storage and reads.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keeping the dates and authors of two policy updates helps distinguish an older suggestion from a later official notice instead of blending them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02002">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02002-mem-plus-plus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-107269a5af712c2f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:mem-plus-plus" data-paper-title="Mem++: Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term Organizational LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b68bb4b0178000af">Why filter by the question&#x27;s time before reading instead of telling the model not to use future information afterward?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amem-plus-plus">Mem++: Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term Organizational LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The University of Texas at Austin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Future documents can influence the model once they enter context, even with an instruction not to use them. Time eligibility first restricts lexical and semantic ranking to documents available then. Retaining verbatim text, date, and author aids audit but does not guarantee retrieval of the right record.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A March organizational decision cannot use an April announcement, however similar it is, as evidence of what was known in March.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02002">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02002-mem-plus-plus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b68bb4b0178000af">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:mem-plus-plus" data-paper-title="Mem++: Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term Organizational LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-54c975b84b7d4d1c">Why keep both lexical and semantic ranking in Mem++?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amem-plus-plus">Mem++: Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term Organizational LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The University of Texas at Austin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Lexical retrieval is good for exact names, IDs, and quotations. Semantic retrieval handles paraphrases and vocabulary changes. Fusion uses both on time-eligible original records and cannot create missing facts. Returned evidence may overlap or conflict, so the final answer must verify contents and provenance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A ticket number can hit lexically. A query about the last database outage may match a record saying storage service interruption semantically.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02002">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02002-mem-plus-plus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-54c975b84b7d4d1c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:mem-plus-plus" data-paper-title="Mem++: Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term Organizational LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-5d808cecfe06482e">Did the local full-write and hybrid-retrieval test run OrgMemBench or an external embedding service?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amem-plus-plus">Mem++: Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term Organizational LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The University of Texas at Austin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It runs verbatim retention, as-of filtering, and a reference lexical-semantic blend. Three seeds verify mechanism invariants. Organizational memory outcomes are the authors&#x27; benchmark; preset vectors and fixed records do not establish real assistant gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A future record being filtered verifies the date rule. Without real organizational QA and encoders, there is no comparable OrgMemBench capability score.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02002">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02002-mem-plus-plus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5d808cecfe06482e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:causal-memory-policy" data-paper-title="Causal Memory Policy: Making Memory Utility Identifiable by Intervening on Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-causal-memory-policy-919f3b4b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b097fb0b5356bc68">Why measure a memory&#x27;s effect on execution before cleaning up a library?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acausal-memory-policy">Causal Memory Policy: Making Memory Utility Identifiable by Intervening on Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Illinois Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Memory takes context and may help, hinder, or be irrelevant. Deletion needs evidence of outcome utility. CMP makes utility estimable with retrieval-exposure experiments and retains uncertain items. It studies interventions under a fixed design, not frequency-based archiving.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two old guides are both frequent. One helps recover from errors and the other repeats background. Outcome comparisons support keeping them differently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02070">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02070-causal-memory-policy/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b097fb0b5356bc68">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:causal-memory-policy" data-paper-title="Causal Memory Policy: Making Memory Utility Identifiable by Intervening on Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-34b255d1bf60271a">Why not delete a memory just because it often appears in failed tasks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acausal-memory-policy">Causal Memory Policy: Making Memory Utility Identifiable by Intervening on Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Illinois Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Hard tasks can preferentially retrieve that memory, biasing the correlation. Balanced randomized exposure gives comparable treatment and control observations, and standard errors protect uncertain items. Replacing one entry in fixed slots changes exposure of others, so the effect is specific to the design rather than universally additive.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A manual used in the hardest incidents can have low success because incidents are difficult. Randomized exposure helps test whether the manual itself hurts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02070">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02070-causal-memory-policy/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-34b255d1bf60271a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:causal-memory-policy" data-paper-title="Causal Memory Policy: Making Memory Utility Identifiable by Intervening on Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-732a00c0f611285c">How does protecting uncertain memories differ from deleting any with a negative estimated mean?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acausal-memory-policy">Causal Memory Policy: Making Memory Utility Identifiable by Intervening on Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Illinois Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>With high variance and few samples, a negative mean can conceal a positive effect. CMP combines standard errors with asymmetric deletion cost, refuses estimates with inadequate support, and returns noop under infinite uncertainty. One negative outcome is not permanent forgetting.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two treatment runs that happen to fail are insufficient to prove harm. Wide uncertainty calls for retention or more evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02070">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02070-causal-memory-policy/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-732a00c0f611285c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:causal-memory-policy" data-paper-title="Causal Memory Policy: Making Memory Utility Identifiable by Intervening on Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7827f7cfea1dba11">Why do fixed k exposure slots prevent interpreting effects as independent additive coefficients?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acausal-memory-policy">Causal Memory Policy: Making Memory Utility Identifiable by Intervening on Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Illinois Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Exposing one more memory changes the others&#x27; distribution inside fixed slots. The measured effect includes replacement under the randomized design. Each row has k entries, column exposures are roughly balanced, and each arm needs at least two observations. Recovering synthetic utilities is not a long-term cross-query policy or real QA accuracy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: In two slots, adding A displaces another candidate. The result measures the net effect of A replacing some content, not A&#x27;s isolated contribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02070">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02070-causal-memory-policy/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7827f7cfea1dba11">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:belief-state-pos" data-paper-title="Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-belief-state-pos-6f953573" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-185b1b94efca0b3a">Why does explicit belief track both facts and unresolved requirements?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abelief-state-pos">Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Facts describe the currently believed world; unresolved requirements describe what the task still lacks. History text alone can mask repeated work as progress. An explicit set supports stall detection, but entries need evidence before removal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: The user&#x27;s address is known, while inventory is unconfirmed. Rereading the address does not resolve inventory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01415">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.01415-belief-state-pos/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-185b1b94efca0b3a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:belief-state-pos" data-paper-title="Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-cd2d64d0824632e7">Why do explicit unresolved requirements detect stalls more easily than a history summary?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abelief-state-pos">Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A summary describes work done. Unresolved requirements make progress comparable. If successive actions do not reduce them, the agent may be cycling and can recover around the specific gap. Action count is not progress. Facts and requirements must update from actual observations, not confidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Five searches still have not verified a date. The unresolved item exposes that activity did not move the goal forward.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01415">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.01415-belief-state-pos/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cd2d64d0824632e7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:belief-state-pos" data-paper-title="Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-381bd7fc8171700f">How does Belief Trapping differ from checking for repeated actions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abelief-state-pos">Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Action repetition checks surface behavior. Belief stalling checks whether unresolved requirements decrease. Different actions can circle the same bad assumption, and the same query may help after a state change. Diagnose progress from facts and requirements, not action strings alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Three search phrases fail to confirm payment despite different wording. Checking again after a transaction settles may actually make progress.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01415">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.01415-belief-state-pos/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-381bd7fc8171700f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:belief-state-pos" data-paper-title="Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-de1c8d589bc7bfa8">Does Δ|unresolved|≥0 prove a task is unsolvable?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Abelief-state-pos">Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It means that the window did not reduce outstanding requirements. Necessary preparation, missing evidence, or a bad updater can cause it. Trigger targeted recovery rather than declaring unsatisfiability. The local run tests belief updates and stall detection without external tools or learned extraction; rule activation is not long-horizon success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Preparing identity verification may leave requirements unchanged but enable the next query. Stopping immediately would cut off a legal path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01415">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.01415-belief-state-pos/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-de1c8d589bc7bfa8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:autocompact" data-paper-title="AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-autocompact-45b25080" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-caf61923d5bef656">Why shouldn&#x27;t a long-horizon coding agent wait until context is full before considering compression?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aautocompact">AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Work includes pending edits, test feedback, and delivery requirements. Bad timing can discard precisely what the next step needs. AutoCompact learns when to compress and how to continue, aiming for task continuity under context pressure rather than shorter text alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Forced compression just after a failing test appears may drop the key error before its cause is recorded. Choose timing with task progress in mind.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02163">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02163-autocompact/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-caf61923d5bef656">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:autocompact" data-paper-title="AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-93322668d5d24082">Why should a judge correct compression timing, summary content, and next action together?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aautocompact">AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>These decisions interact. Early compression can lose evidence, missing facts can induce bad actions, and later behavior can squander a correct summary. Executing the corrected tuple lets training observe joint consequences. Summary fluency alone cannot establish sufficiency for long-horizon coding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A clear summary omitting a parameter constraint can cause the next edit to break an interface. Correct both memory and action.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02163">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02163-autocompact/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-93322668d5d24082">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:autocompact" data-paper-title="AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a097c49f032f7e2a">What is the trade-off between learned compression timing and a fixed length threshold?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aautocompact">AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A fixed threshold responds only to capacity and cannot distinguish moments with fragile commitments or unfinished work. A learned decision can use task state but requires reliable supervision and can err. Evaluate actual downstream coding results and cost alongside context reduction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Compression just after a tool return and before recording its conclusion is risky. Waiting until state is clear can preserve what matters.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02163">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02163-autocompact/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a097c49f032f7e2a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:autocompact" data-paper-title="AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-dd8fc5de66dd4f65">After a judge corrects the tuple, should the environment execute the original action or the corrected one?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aautocompact">AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Execute the corrected decision, summary, and action together so training records match consequences. SFT plus outcome RL needs real execution feedback. The local run verifies the three-field in-place correction contract without training a coding agent or running SWE containers. Field checks are not code-repair results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: If the judge changes &#x27;submit now&#x27; to &#x27;run the failing test first,&#x27; executing the old submit action makes its reward invalid evidence for the corrected policy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02163">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.02163-autocompact/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dd8fc5de66dd4f65">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memfit" data-paper-title="MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memfit-d14853dc" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4b853f8ead5db496">Why does MemFit focus on write costs for high-frequency conversations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemfit">MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A long-lived assistant continually receives turns. Rewriting all memory with a costly model on every turn incurs cost before retrieval and can erase details. MemFit keeps writes lightweight and originals traceable, moving query-specific filtering to reads while facing the growing index size.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A support system gains hundreds of turns per day, many never queried. Complex semantic rewriting of each turn can cost more than useful future queries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.00872-memfit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4b853f8ead5db496">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memfit" data-paper-title="MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b9ff61056b142ab1">Why store append-only raw turns separately from searchable segment summaries?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemfit">MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Summaries make compact indexes but can omit details. Keeping raw records unchanged gives later close reading traceable evidence. Writes avoid expensive model rewrites of all history; reads combine lexical, semantic, and reranking signals. An index hit is only an entry point, and an omitted summary detail may still exist.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A segment summary says payment API discussion. Read the original turn to find the exact timeout; keeping only the summary might lose it permanently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.00872-memfit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b9ff61056b142ab1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memfit" data-paper-title="MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e107e4a047780dea">What does inexpensive append-only writing trade off against LLM memory rewriting every turn?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemfit">MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Append-only avoids repeated generation and irreversible rewriting, but raw storage grows and retrieval and indexing do more filtering. LLM writes can abstract early but lose details. Compare writing, storage, and final retrieval quality together, not just call counts in one stage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Saving a thousand raw turns is cheap, but a later query must quickly locate one address change. Inexpensive writes do not guarantee cheap reads.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.00872-memfit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e107e4a047780dea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memfit" data-paper-title="MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-499b4408c327aeaf">Does the local hybrid retrieval hook mean embedding and cross-encoder inference ran?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemfit">MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The hook accepts lexical, semantic, and reranking signals but does not call a real embedder or cross-encoder. It tests append-only behavior and score combination. Fixture semantic scores cannot establish real long-conversation retrieval quality or paper latency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Correctly sorting three records with preset semantic scores tests fusion, not whether a model derives reliable scores from natural language.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2610.00872-memfit/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-499b4408c327aeaf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:upliftmem" data-paper-title="UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-upliftmem-e7065d9f" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8147d2ef26cbd835">Why does UpliftMem distinguish relevant retrieval from helping the agent complete a task?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aupliftmem">UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beihang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Similar memories can duplicate what is known or conflict with other records. Relevance scores need not measure execution value. UpliftMem asks whether a complete set gives a fixed executor additional benefit, reserving context for evidence combinations that change outcomes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Three high-similarity records give the right API name but omit authentication. The task still fails, so similarity alone does not establish utility.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36805">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.36805-upliftmem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8147d2ef26cbd835">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:upliftmem" data-paper-title="UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9be80c53f396be47">Why isn&#x27;t the utility of a memory set the sum of individual relevance scores?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aupliftmem">UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beihang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Items can complement, duplicate, or conflict, so set-level execution effects are not additive relevance. The method supervises on the difference with and without memory for the same frozen executor. Additional rollouts go where they can change the local choice. Relevance proposes candidates, not measured uplift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: One item gives an API name and another its argument constraints; together they enable execution. Two similar copies of the API introduction may be less useful.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36805">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.36805-upliftmem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9be80c53f396be47">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:upliftmem" data-paper-title="UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-247598bcebcf4e66">How does EVSI allocation differ from giving each candidate the same number of extra rollouts?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aupliftmem">UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beihang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Uniform allocation ignores whether uncertainty can change the selection. EVSI asks how much an observation is expected to change the local retrieval decision. A correlated Gaussian posterior expresses candidate dependencies. This allocates budget; the highest predicted mean is not observed success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Extra probing is low-value when two sets are far apart. A rollout can be more useful for two close, uncertain alternatives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36805">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.36805-upliftmem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-247598bcebcf4e66">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:upliftmem" data-paper-title="UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fb77451d166994c2">Why does set_level_uplift require paired treatment and control?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aupliftmem">UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beihang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Compare memory versus no memory on the same task, frozen executor, and matched conditions to reduce task and model confounds. The local run implements paired differences and EVSI on a fixed posterior, not full set construction, shared scoring, or real execution. Component outputs are not agent success gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A memory set on a hard problem versus no memory on an easy one is not comparable. Both conditions must face the same instance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36805">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.36805-upliftmem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fb77451d166994c2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:remem" data-paper-title="ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-remem-598e18f2" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8426a6e9fbacaf9f">Why are the input challenges of long-context recommendation agents broader than long history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aremem">ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong Polytechnic University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The agent must understand heterogeneous item pages and track preferences through accumulating user behavior. Errors on either side can lead to poor recommendations. ReMem studies perception and evolving memory together to provide enough decision evidence within a fixed budget, not simply add history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Product weight is embedded in an image and the user now prefers light items. Shorter chat history alone neither reads the weight nor guarantees an updated preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37311">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.37311-remem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8426a6e9fbacaf9f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:remem" data-paper-title="ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-40acc119d72f0bd6">Why improve both item perception and bounded memory in a recommendation agent instead of only shortening history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aremem">ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong Polytechnic University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Bad page extraction makes even a sophisticated preference memory retain wrong semantics. OCR perception first produces compact item representations, then dynamic memory updates preferences under budget. Several memory views share policy training while supplying distinct evidence. Test preference answers must never be injected to create apparent gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A price in small print on an image cannot be corrected by compressing browsing history. Extract reliable attributes first, then retain information relevant to the user&#x27;s budget.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37311">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.37311-remem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-40acc119d72f0bd6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:remem" data-paper-title="ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e31f4ffd2401e801">What is the trade-off between dynamic fixed-budget memory and full history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aremem">ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong Polytechnic University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Full history retains more but costs grow with interactions. Dynamic memory ranks by relevance and recency and emphasizes current preferences within budget, at the risk of losing rare important constraints. Recent observations do not replace auditing long-term facts, and real user episodes are needed to measure recommendation quality.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Recent running-shoe purchases should not erase a longstanding material allergy. Verify the constraint survived compression.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37311">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.37311-remem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e31f4ffd2401e801">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:remem" data-paper-title="ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-4a97e3877c77acd7">Why can&#x27;t Multi-Memory GRPO mix all memory views into one advantage group?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aremem">ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · The Hong Kong Polytechnic University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Normalize rewards separately within each memory view for the same query, then share the clipped policy update. Mixing views can confuse differences in view difficulty with action advantage. The local run tests budget, temporal updates, and objectives, not OCR, browsers, or real recommendation episodes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Sparse views may have lower rewards overall. Mixing them with rich views can wrongly attribute that difficulty to particular responses.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37311">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.37311-remem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4a97e3877c77acd7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:context-lm" data-paper-title="Context Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-context-lm-ca518f91" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-1b83f4d20e64d534">Why is a context file part of model behavior rather than a fixed external summary?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acontext-lm">Context Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta Superintelligence Labs</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The model chooses what to keep, delete, and reorganize; later actions read the edited state. In a fixed harness, external rules choose what and when to compress. Model editing changes responsibility and risks losing important constraints, so capacity and execution contracts still matter.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Delete an obsolete log and keep its conclusion proactively instead of waiting for a length threshold to summarize all history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37725">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.37725-context-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1b83f4d20e64d534">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:context-lm" data-paper-title="Context Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7eb6f092d33d44b2">Why does letting a model edit a context file also change KV reuse cost?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acontext-lm">Context Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta Superintelligence Labs</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The file prefix determines whether cached representations still match. Changing early tokens usually requires re-prefilling the suffix. File transforms therefore determine both what to remember and future runtime cost. Shorter text is not always cheaper when it invalidates a large cache.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Appending an observation at the end can preserve prefix KV. Rewriting the opening summary can force recomputation despite fewer total words.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37725">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.37725-context-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7eb6f092d33d44b2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:context-lm" data-paper-title="Context Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-84c99bee2b5a6493">How do context editing and direct KV eviction differ in what logical history remains?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acontext-lm">Context Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta Superintelligence Labs</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>File edits change the logical token sequence the model sees and require prefix matching before reuse. Direct KV eviction can retain logical text while changing active cache state. Reducing active context in both cases does not imply the same cache identity or recovery semantics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Deleting early file text changes the prefix for all later tokens, so the old full KV cannot be copied. Dropping KV alone can leave the text intact.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37725">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.37725-context-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-84c99bee2b5a6493">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:context-lm" data-paper-title="Context Language Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-02bd02e85b8213dc">Why must suffix cache reuse recompute from the first token mismatch?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acontext-lm">Context Language Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Washington / Meta Superintelligence Labs</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Causal hidden states depend on earlier tokens. After the first mismatch, later identical text can still have different KV. Keep only the longest common prefix and check file capacity explicitly. The local run tests edits and boundaries without CLM training or a long multi-agent swarm.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Changing token 100 can alter token 101 and all following states, not just the replaced position.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37725">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2609.37725-context-lm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-02bd02e85b8213dc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:mnemon" data-paper-title="Mnemon: Raw Records, Fast Judgments, Slow Thoughts" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-mnemon-dd3564ee" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f832a1b58f4143d5">Why does Mnemon keep dated originals but give the answering model only a small view?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amnemon">Mnemon: Raw Records, Fast Judgments, Slow Thoughts</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文未列机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Originals retain checkable details and dates. A small view gives relevant evidence within budget instead of replaying all history. Slow planning proposes searches and fast Jev decisions select records. Missing facts may require further lookup; the view is not a lossless summary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Pick a few dated rescheduling events from years of records rather than resend all chats to answer when the latest change happened.</p>
