The prior bounds updates, while the residual adapts to current memory. It learns from executed routes only and is not guaranteed to beat the prior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A base route favors generic retrieval, but the residual learns from current tool tasks to favor an experience store. The language model&#x27;s weights stay frozen.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01739">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2608.01739-coevo-mem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3b67e8e3d352fecb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:coevo-mem" data-paper-title="CoEvo-Mem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-11233bf81c6e4297">Why include task axis and tool signature in a retrieval key instead of reusing by query text alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Acoevo-mem">CoEvo-Mem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 论文未列机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Similar queries may need different routes for different tasks or tool versions. Axis and signature prevent reuse across incompatible contracts. The local run checks rewrite, residual, and alternating update flow. A public mini-suite and Evolve registry entry do not establish full learning or all paper benchmarks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two order lookup services return different schemas. Matching query words do not justify a memory route that uses obsolete fields.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01739">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2608.01739-coevo-mem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-11233bf81c6e4297">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:skillrise" data-paper-title="SkillRise" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-skillrise-fa529938" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d86d7ab30cfa12bb">Why does one policy alternate solving the current task and curating a skill document?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Askillrise">SkillRise</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Solving produces experience; curation passes transferable material directly into the next task, making cross-task learning part of behavior. Related tasks progress from easy to hard, so documents must help later rather than simply explain present success. This is not independent episode training and not a mandate to keep all experiences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: After a simple file search, record location and verification methods for a harder modification task instead of copying the old answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.26784-skillrise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d86d7ab30cfa12bb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:skillrise" data-paper-title="SkillRise" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9386b52986589e13">Why reward skill-document curation from later tasks rather than current task success?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Askillrise">SkillRise</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Current success mostly reflects solving, not whether the resulting skill helps later users or the same agent. Related tasks form a sequence, and discounted downstream returns supervise curation toward transferable experience. Apply the two phase advantages to their own generated tokens rather than broadcasting credit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A lucky correct answer can still yield a reusable testing procedure. Its curation value is visible only if it helps later tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.26784-skillrise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9386b52986589e13">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:skillrise" data-paper-title="SkillRise" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e88f05c7ec0f5b77">How does a connected curriculum transfer experience differently from training episodes independently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Askillrise">SkillRise</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A skill document curated from one task becomes input to the next, so transferable experience can be used and evaluated. Independent episodes normally do not expose this link. Related tasks can overfit a curriculum; distinguish downstream document benefit from current solving and do not infer generalization from transfer counts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A simple table cleanup produces checks for a constrained variant next. Random unrelated tasks may never use those checks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.26784-skillrise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e88f05c7ec0f5b77">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:skillrise" data-paper-title="SkillRise" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6488d5dae7432edc">Do local document-update and downstream-credit counts mean Qwen3 was trained with RL?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Askillrise">SkillRise</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Zhejiang University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Controlled PlanBench tests state evolution, skill transfer, and phase-specific credit without Qwen3 training or the paper&#x27;s three environments. Writes show the action happened, not parameter learning. Perfect mini-suite scores are not comparable with paper Pass@k.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Deterministic rules can write 120 documents. Without real gradient updates, that is not the paper&#x27;s shared-policy training.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26784">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.26784-skillrise/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6488d5dae7432edc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:unimem" data-paper-title="UniMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-unimem-c304c78e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ceb2875337a2818b">Why can&#x27;t UniMem handle streaming tasks with fixed weights alone or by accumulating raw episodes indefinitely?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aunimem">UniMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · CASIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed weights cannot promptly absorb new situations. Raw episodes create growing retrieval and context costs. UniMem combines recent examples with stable recurring knowledge to adapt and reuse experience. Timeliness and stability matter, and frequent patterns are not necessarily correct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Record a new service&#x27;s first interface change as a specific event. Only after a rule continues to hold is it a candidate for a stable habit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26017">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.26017-unimem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ceb2875337a2818b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:unimem" data-paper-title="UniMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3cf08ee16e225a73">Why first keep new tasks in an episodic buffer and consolidate only repeated reliable patterns?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aunimem">UniMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · CASIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An isolated event may be noise or exceptional. Episodic storage preserves context; repeated reliable patterns are better candidates for stable parametric knowledge. Self-routing chooses how to use both. Repetition needs reliability checks so recurring mistakes are not consolidated as rules.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Record the first temporary outage as an event. Only repeatedly confirmed configuration constraints should become a general pattern.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26017">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.26017-unimem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3cf08ee16e225a73">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:unimem" data-paper-title="UniMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-1d5877beb700c4b8">What is the trade-off between episodic retrieval and parametric memory for updates and use?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aunimem">UniMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · CASIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Episodic entries are easy to append, audit, and delete, but reads consume retrieval and context. Parametric memory internalizes recurring patterns for direct use, but individual facts are harder to undo. The approaches are complementary; consolidation is not merely copying tables and can accumulate errors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keep a temporary meeting date as traceable episodic memory. A stable tool-use pattern may be worth consolidating and changes less often.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26017">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.26017-unimem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1d5877beb700c4b8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:unimem" data-paper-title="UniMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b04dee9b415912bf">Does the local parametric route actually extend LLM weight blocks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Aunimem">UniMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · CASIA</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Local parametric memory is a structured pattern table that tests thresholds, episodic-to-consolidated routing, and counts. It neither trains nor expands model weights. Consolidation counts and deterministic success do not establish LLM internalization or streaming capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Adding a rule after three occurrences is a state transition. If model weights did not change, it is not parametric learning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26017">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.26017-unimem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b04dee9b415912bf">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hiskill" data-paper-title="HiSkill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-hiskill-6a9652b8" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6f93afb88c05bebc">Why are high-level skills and AtomicOps different node types?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahiskill">HiSkill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>High-level skills describe goals and reusable procedures. AtomicOps are executable actions linked through decomposition. Treating both as text snippets blurs abstract plans and immediately executable actions. Ground operations using current state and tool contracts rather than executing a high-level name.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Organize orders is high level; query, verify status, and write output are atomic operations that can become legal calls after decomposition.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25853">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.25853-hiskill/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6f93afb88c05bebc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hiskill" data-paper-title="HiSkill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-01a662c9411b2245">Why distinguish decomposition, temporal, and recovery edges in a skill graph?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahiskill">HiSkill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Decomposition maps a high-level goal to AtomicOps; temporal edges constrain ordering; recovery edges provide failure paths. A generic similarity edge would lose execution semantics. After retrieving a subgraph, ground it in current state. Finding a skill name is not action completion.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Upload decomposes into selecting and submitting a file. A failure can follow a recovery edge to refresh login; doing that as a universal prerequisite is unnecessary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25853">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.25853-hiskill/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-01a662c9411b2245">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hiskill" data-paper-title="HiSkill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-3a39ef5716fcd49d">What is the trade-off between retrieving a relevant skill subgraph and placing the whole graph in context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahiskill">HiSkill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A subgraph limits interpretation and grounding to useful decomposition, order, and recovery relations. The full graph keeps more paths but costs more context and choices. A local subgraph can miss remote prerequisites, so check execution conditions; shorter input is not necessarily better task performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Retrieve the failed upload and nearby recovery nodes. If authentication is absent, the compact subgraph still cannot execute legally.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25853">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.25853-hiskill/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3a39ef5716fcd49d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:hiskill" data-paper-title="HiSkill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f9bf03107aa70202">Does constructing a graph from controlled trajectories show an online LLM learned to extract skill relations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Ahiskill">HiSkill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Local nodes and relations are supplied by controlled traces, testing hierarchy, subgraph retrieval, and reuse without online LLM extraction. AtomicOp reuse counts show real reuse within the fixture, not semantic discovery in open environments or extrapolated token savings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Following a supplied recovery edge tests the graph executor. It does not show a model can infer that edge from an unseen failure log.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25853">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.25853-hiskill/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f9bf03107aa70202">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memcon" data-paper-title="Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memcon-717a2e37" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c3c0d162719c7ac">Why does MemCon make whether to use memory a control action?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemcon">Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未明确标注（正文 HTML 未显示一作机构映射）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retrieval, plan injection, query changes, and maintenance cost work. Some simple tasks are cheaper without memory. MemCon selects based on discrete progress, repetition, and memory size, then learns from terminal success and efficiency. Memory need not run on every turn.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: With an obvious next tool, skip retrieval. After repeated failure and with a relevant successful plan, inject it or search deeper.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13591">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.13591-memcon/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c3c0d162719c7ac">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memcon" data-paper-title="Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8957db0ab44f22e6">Why must the memory controller count UCB visits per discrete state rather than use global action frequencies?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemcon">Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未明确标注（正文 HTML 未显示一作机构映射）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An operation useful early may not help later or under memory pressure. State-local values and counts let the controller learn those trade-offs separately. It explores unvisited actions first, then updates from terminal success and efficiency. No extra LLM call applies to selection; retrieval and execution still have costs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Deep retrieval may help at the start and delay completion near the end. Count attempts separately instead of sharing one global success rate.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13591">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.13591-memcon/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8957db0ab44f22e6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memcon" data-paper-title="Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d2c33c0e1bbf4b0c">What is the trade-off between tabular UCB and asking an LLM to choose a memory policy every round?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemcon">Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未明确标注（正文 HTML 未显示一作机构映射）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tabular control needs no extra model call and has interpretable states and actions, but limited discrete features cannot express arbitrary semantic contexts. LLM control is flexible but costs calls. State-local UCB does not guarantee convergence as the environment and memory change.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A repetition flag can trigger deeper retrieval immediately. Semantically different tasks with the same discrete state may still look identical to the table.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13591">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.13591-memcon/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d2c33c0e1bbf4b0c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memcon" data-paper-title="Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-67d5abfc2cadf284">Can MemCon&#x27;s Q update use sample-mean UCB or TD bootstrapping?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemcon">Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 未明确标注（正文 HTML 未显示一作机构映射）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The local implementation follows v3 state-local counts, discounts terminal success and efficiency by distance, and updates repeated state-action pairs in reverse order. It does not bootstrap future Q. Unvisited actions go first with initial Q tie-breaking. Differences from mutable upstream main counts are documented.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An action seen twice in one episode receives two discounted updates in reverse order, not one reward averaged by visits.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13591">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2607.13591-memcon/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-67d5abfc2cadf284">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memento-skills" data-paper-title="Memento-Skills" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memento-skills-c4d49bbe" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-e28f108866db2db6">What repeated work does Memento-Skills avoid across similar tasks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemento-skills">Memento-Skills</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Memento Team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A run records useful steps, errors, and conditions. Raw logs still need interpretation next time. Memento-Skills makes experience searchable and updatable for reuse. Usefulness depends on applicability and actual execution; storage and version counts do not measure capability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: After discovering a billing date-format issue, reuse a skill with format validation instead of rereading the entire failure log.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18743">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2603.18743-memento-skills/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e28f108866db2db6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memento-skills" data-paper-title="Memento-Skills" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-884b9152b4a7f491">Why are versioned skills more reusable than appending raw execution logs to context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemento-skills">Memento-Skills</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Memento Team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A log describes one run. Structured skills extract applicability and steps for later retrieval. Versioned merge tracks corrections instead of keeping contradictory old copies. Abstraction must preserve provenance and failure conditions; shorter wording does not make it a reliable general procedure.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A deployment log contains temporary directories and retry noise. The skill retains dependency checks and rollback conditions, and a later version fixes obsolete arguments.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18743">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2603.18743-memento-skills/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-884b9152b4a7f491">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memento-skills" data-paper-title="Memento-Skills" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b9e7b86356628ade">How does versioned Merge differ from appending a new skill every time?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemento-skills">Memento-Skills</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Memento Team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Merge integrates feedback into relevant existing skills and records changes rather than accumulating near duplicates. Appending is simpler but can retain contradictory versions. Merge must preserve applicability and check regressions; one topical or successful example does not justify a global replacement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Update an export skill for a pagination limit. If it applies to one service only, keep that condition rather than requiring pagination everywhere.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18743">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2603.18743-memento-skills/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b9e7b86356628ade">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memento-skills" data-paper-title="Memento-Skills" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-84e7bd0f8016135d">What does low local joint success with nonzero skill telemetry show?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemento-skills">Memento-Skills</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Memento Team</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The mechanism ran and many tasks still failed. Creation or reuse counts cannot be cherry-picked as improvement. Local tests cover state updates and fair budgets without the original large model, real web, or full benchmark. Keep negative outcomes with process evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Ten skill retrievals show invocation happened. If the task failed, they do not establish correct content or execution benefit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18743">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2603.18743-memento-skills/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-84e7bd0f8016135d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:u-mem" data-paper-title="U-Mem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-u-mem-1e639ec3" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-38a7caab07361558">Why does U-Mem treat missing knowledge as an active acquisition problem?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Au-mem">U-Mem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Similar memories can omit a necessary fact or procedure. Repeated retrieval can leave the same gap. U-Mem learns to acquire information from self, tools, or experts as needed and considers reuse afterward. New knowledge needs provenance and feedback; an expert label does not guarantee truth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Memory contains only an obsolete API call. Find new documentation for missing arguments instead of returning the old fragment repeatedly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22406">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.22406-u-mem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-38a7caab07361558">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:u-mem" data-paper-title="U-Mem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4c22d63ec43b7864">Why escalate acquisition from self or teacher to tool research to an expert instead of always asking the strongest expert?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Au-mem">U-Mem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Costs differ. Try cheaper potentially adequate paths first and reserve costly help for persistent uncertainty. Thompson sampling combines historical utility and uncertainty, and memory is verified before writing. The cascade orders value and cost decisions, not a claim that cheap sources are always correct.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Check memory for common configuration, then docs, then an expert only if ambiguity remains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22406">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.22406-u-mem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4c22d63ec43b7864">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:u-mem" data-paper-title="U-Mem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ecb60d81ada577f1">How does semantic similarity plus Thompson sampling differ from ranking memory by similarity alone?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Au-mem">U-Mem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Similarity favors related content. Beta posterior samples explore uncertain memories that may be useful, then outcomes update the posterior. This is not random insertion of irrelevant material. The uncertainty–relevance balance depends on real feedback rather than confidence alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two records are equally related, one well tested and one new. Sampling can occasionally test the newer one instead of always selecting the highest old score.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22406">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.22406-u-mem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ecb60d81ada577f1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:u-mem" data-paper-title="U-Mem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-14d3f0283f16c6fd">What limits follow from deterministic local experts and knowledge sources?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Au-mem">U-Mem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · National University of Singapore</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They omit real search failures, hallucination, paid models, and token cost. They verify escalation, validation, writes, and proxy cost accounting only. Receiving preset correct knowledge after low confidence does not reproduce HotpotQA, AIME, or real savings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A fixture expert always returns a supplied fact. That tests escalation control flow, not real expert request success or cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式与算法, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22406">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.22406-u-mem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-14d3f0283f16c6fd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:pahf" data-paper-title="Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-pahf-5582b2a9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-cc0d33bd49105a98">Why do pre-action clarification and post-action correction complement each other?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Apahf">Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / Princeton University（工作完成于 Meta）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Clarify unknown or uncertain preferences before acting to reduce guesses. Feedback after execution corrects the action and stale memory, handling drift. A confident old belief is not grounds to reject correction when preferences change by context or time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Someone formerly liked spicy food but wants mild today. Ask first if uncertain; if an order is already wrong, update based on the explicit correction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16173">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.16173-pahf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cc0d33bd49105a98">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:pahf" data-paper-title="Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ed0c2c2164e5bf6a">Why allow users to correct preferences after action even when prior memory is confident?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Apahf">Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / Princeton University（工作完成于 Meta）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Confidence describes current memory, not whether preferences changed with time or context. Retrieval and clarification before action address uncertainty; afterward correction replaces stale content. Accepting feedback only at low confidence can permanently lock in learned mistakes or drifted preferences.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A user previously preferred early flights but changed routines. Update the preference after rejection rather than booking early flights on old confidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16173">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.16173-pahf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ed0c2c2164e5bf6a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:pahf" data-paper-title="Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-48e5888ea773945f">How does explicit preference memory differ from providing a hidden user persona as ground truth?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Apahf">Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / Princeton University（工作完成于 Meta）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Memory comes from actual user feedback and has observable provenance. Hidden persona or gold action belongs only to evaluation. Giving it early removes the personalization problem. PAHF learns preferences and drift through interactions rather than reading a test specification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Store that a user said they avoid coffee on workdays. Do not feed the identical statement from a hidden fixture before interaction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16173">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.16173-pahf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-48e5888ea773945f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:pahf" data-paper-title="Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b7a9fbb39023c495">Why keep current context and remembered preference together in PAHF policy input?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Apahf">Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta Superintelligence Labs / Princeton University（工作完成于 Meta）</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Actions depend on instructions, observations, explicit memory, and pre-action feedback. A preference is not a context-free global command. Tie new feedback to its context to avoid converting one situational change into a permanent rule. The local implementation tests memory and feedback contracts, not the original robot or shopping simulator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Selecting sugar-free drinks for guests today does not necessarily change personal taste. Keep the scene to understand correction scope.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16173">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.16173-pahf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b7a9fbb39023c495">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memskill" data-paper-title="MemSkill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memskill-ffe2092a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-82b492a82fb86598">Why turn one-off experiences into callable operational knowledge in MemSkill?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemskill">MemSkill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Episodic memory records what happened, while later tasks may need repeatable steps, preconditions, and recovery. MemSkill extracts skills and lets execution select relevant memories. Over-abstraction can lose conditions, and repeated success is not universal applicability. Check transfer through actual execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A spreadsheet repair includes long dialogue. Future work needs check column names before date conversion and the conditions where that rule applies.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02474">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.02474-memskill/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-82b492a82fb86598">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memskill" data-paper-title="MemSkill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c0f675d6e105b894">Why are controller memory selection and designer skill compilation different jobs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemskill">MemSkill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Selection decides which experiences the current task reads. Compilation turns recurring successes into reusable procedures on a longer timescale. Feedback also drives versions. One retrieved success does not establish that every detail should be consolidated; distinguish reusable steps from incidental conditions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Retrieve a prior fix for today&#x27;s error and compile a skill only after confirming a repeated pattern. Do not hard-code a temporary account from one log.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02474">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.02474-memskill/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c0f675d6e105b894">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memskill" data-paper-title="MemSkill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-07fecf19d9da77a6">Why is repeated success stronger evidence for consolidation than a single successful trace?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemskill">MemSkill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One success may depend on chance or hidden help. Repetition supports a pattern across instances and makes it a better skill candidate. It does not prove causal necessity; inspect prerequisites, failures, and version changes. Frequency does not replace validation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Three successes clear cache first because those tasks may all need it. Record the condition rather than mandate clearing cache everywhere.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02474">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.02474-memskill/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-07fecf19d9da77a6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memskill" data-paper-title="MemSkill" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-69a2bd22598ec1e6">What is the evidence boundary between local skill-version updates and full designer learning?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemskill">MemSkill</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The local run verifies selection, compilation-style transitions, versions, and budgets without the paper&#x27;s LLM, RL, or real environment. Version increments show the path ran, not reliable skill extraction from natural-language logs. Perfect controlled scores are not paper cross-task ability.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Rules can convert recurring steps to a template for a pipeline test. Without a learned designer, do not claim open-task procedure discovery.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02474">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2602.02474-memskill/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-69a2bd22598ec1e6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:sage" data-paper-title="SAGE" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-sage-ae754679" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-52bc9ca93fa82930">Why make use of accumulated skills a learning objective in SAGE?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asage">SAGE</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Stored skills need timely, correct selection and can harm when mismatched. SAGE connects experience-derived skills to retrieval and uses later outcomes to govern their lifecycle. It studies durable use of experience, not library size or successful trace count.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A migration skill is irrelevant to looking up one row. Knowing when not to invoke it is useful skill selection.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.17102">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2512.17102-sage/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-52bc9ca93fa82930">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:sage" data-paper-title="SAGE" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-b5c319a86b79af83">Why revise or retire skills from successful trajectories after later failures?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asage">SAGE</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Success establishes utility under past conditions, not new ones. Returns train selection and reveal obsolete content. Revision and eviction stop accumulation of errors. An append-only library can keep retrieving relevant-looking stale skills and reinforce incorrect behavior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A download skill worked before a site redesign. Update or disable it rather than rank it first based on old success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.17102">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2512.17102-sage/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b5c319a86b79af83">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:sage" data-paper-title="SAGE" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ffb4ccd96e5b0cbb">How does learned retrieval qφ differ from fixed semantic nearest neighbors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asage">SAGE</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Semantic nearest neighbors use description similarity. Learned retrieval adapts to which skills improve execution returns. Outcomes are confounded by environment and task difficulty, so success after invocation is not independent causal contribution. Inspect updates with bank state and visible evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two skills sound like file organization. A more reliable route can get a higher learned score even if it shares fewer words.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.17102">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2512.17102-sage/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ffb4ccd96e5b0cbb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:sage" data-paper-title="SAGE" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-22f204cc4f69319a">Can SAGE and sage-planner share implementation conclusions because they have the same name?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Asage">SAGE</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Wisconsin–Madison</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. SAGE concerns an RL-driven skill library; sage-planner concerns symbolic action gates and suffix edits. The local SAGE run tests skill state and budgets, without paper-scale models or benchmarks. Shared names do not fill evidence gaps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A skill-library revision invokes no symbolic gate. Gate tests from the other method cannot verify this one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.17102">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2512.17102-sage/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-22f204cc4f69319a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:legomem" data-paper-title="LEGOMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-legomem-3e37af3a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c4c27071fd8d1be5">Why does LegoMem focus on recurring workflows with multiple roles and steps?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alegomem">LEGOMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Office workflows share portions but change goals and roles. Reorganizable procedures let new tasks reuse the right steps rather than copy one complete run. Units must retain dependencies and context; pieces that look composable can still lack inputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Weekly reports and project briefs both need collection and source verification, but different approvers. Reuse collection and replan handoff.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04851">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2510.04851-legomem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c4c27071fd8d1be5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:legomem" data-paper-title="LEGOMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-21c86cef36853d28">Why separate orchestration and execution memory for recombination on new tasks?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alegomem">LEGOMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Decomposition and delegation capture high-level dependencies, while action templates ground calls. One full trace binds them to particular people and environments. Layers can reuse structure while swapping execution units. Admit verified units only and recheck interfaces and prerequisites when combining them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Collect, verify, and summarize stays the same while data comes from a database in one task and a file in another.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04851">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2510.04851-legomem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-21c86cef36853d28">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:legomem" data-paper-title="LEGOMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-2732f77db1bafc8e">What generalization trade-off separates procedural recombination from whole-trace retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alegomem">LEGOMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Whole traces preserve complete context but may be tied to one task. Procedural units recombine for new needs but can lose cross-unit prerequisites. Legal dependencies and validation are needed; individual success does not imply arbitrary compositions work.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Reading a spreadsheet and sending email may both work alone. Verify recipients and data permissions before combining.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04851">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2510.04851-legomem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2732f77db1bafc8e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:legomem" data-paper-title="LEGOMem" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-8e26df792894a3d7">Does local reused_plans verify real multi-agent Office delegation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Alegomem">LEGOMem</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Microsoft Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. The local run extracts action/domain units from structured verifiable plans and reuses high-level and fine-grained steps. It does not execute Office apps, LLM delegation, or complete recovery. Reuse counts are neither OfficeBench success nor real tool cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: A rule reuses a subplan 100 times without showing a model can delegate between real document and email apps.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式与算法, 本地复现, 复现边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04851">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2510.04851-legomem/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8e26df792894a3d7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memtool" data-paper-title="MemTool" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<span id="paper-agent-research-memtool-13c64e5c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-30295a2477bae0ec">Why do tool descriptions need bounded dynamic memory?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemtool">MemTool</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · PricewaterhouseCoopers Commercial Technology and Innovation Office</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>MCP schemas and instructions consume context, while static truncation can remove tools in use. MemTool protects current workflow requirements and manages other descriptions dynamically. Preserve executable interfaces rather than maximizing removals.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: An order lookup followed by refund still needs the refund tool even if it was not called recently.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21428">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2507.21428-memtool/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-30295a2477bae0ec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="agent-research:memtool" data-paper-title="MemTool" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="agent-research" data-theme="agent-research" data-topic="agent-research/memory-and-skills">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Agents / Memory and skills: retrieval, reuse, and invalidation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-356e892465a4deff">Why protect workflow-required tools before considering recency or historic success?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=agent-research%3Amemtool">MemTool</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · PricewaterhouseCoopers Commercial Technology and Innovation Office</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retention scores reflect past usage and may undervalue an uncalled but required future tool. Protect dependencies first, then evict lower-scoring unprotected entries. If required tools exceed capacity, silent truncation does not preserve a valid workflow.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Upload is required at the end of archiving even if not recently used. Do not remove it solely for low recency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式与算法. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21428">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../agent-research/2507.21428-memtool/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-356e892465a4deff">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
